summaries.example: Imagine that Maya writes a diary about her feelings. She may choose to show parts to a trusted friend, but she does not want everyone at school to read it. Privacy can give Maya a quiet place, protect her information, and let her decide what to share.
summaries.summary: Privacy means having protection from unwanted watching, listening, sharing, or interference. It can include being left alone, controlling personal information, having a private place, and making personal decisions. The entry explains that people have not always drawn the line between public and private in the same way. In older theories, the household was often separated from public political life. Later thinkers connected privacy with freedom and personal choice. Modern technology has made privacy harder to protect because devices and companies can collect, combine, and use large amounts of data. The entry also describes disagreements. Some philosophers think privacy can be explained by other rights, such as property or bodily safety. Others think privacy is a group of connected interests with its own importance. Feminist thinkers point out that calling the home private has sometimes protected unfair power and abuse, while removing privacy completely could also allow too much government control. Privacy may protect friendship, trust, independence, and democracy, so it matters to society as well as to individuals.
key_ideas: Privacy does not have only one meaning. It can involve a home, a body, personal choices, relationships, or information.
Ideas about what is private and public have changed across history and cultures.
Phones, apps, cameras, and other technologies can collect information and make profiles about people.
Privacy can help people form friendships, think freely, and take part in community and democratic life.
Some thinkers say privacy is made of several different interests rather than one single right.
Privacy can protect people, but the idea of privacy has also sometimes hidden unfair treatment or harm inside homes and families.
summaries.why_it_matters: Privacy helps people have places to rest, relationships in which they can choose what to share, and freedom to think and act without constant observation. It also raises difficult questions about technology, safety, fairness, and power. Understanding privacy can help us ask who collects information, who can use it, and whether a rule protects people equally.

important_terms.definition: Having some space, information, or decisions protected from unwanted attention or interference.
The part of life connected with government, school, work, or other shared activities.
The part of life connected with home, family, personal choices, and things people may not want widely known.
Personal information, such as a name, location, health detail, or message, that a person may want to control.
The ability to make choices and guide your own life.

questions_to_think_about: Should a school app be allowed to collect a student’s location? Why or why not?
Is something private just because it happens at home?
Can sharing information with one person still be private?
How can rules protect privacy without hiding unfair treatment?
Why might privacy matter for people making their own choices?

summaries.example: Suppose a fitness app records a teenager’s location, exercise, sleep, and health information. Sharing a step count with friends may fit the expectations of that relationship, while sending the same data to advertisers or an employer may not. The issue is not simply whether the data is secret. It concerns who receives it, for what purpose, under which rules, and what conclusions can be drawn about the person.
summaries.summary: The entry presents privacy as a broad and disputed concept rather than a single, settled right. Historically, privacy has been discussed through the division between public political life and private domestic life, through control of personal information, and through legal protections. These histories overlap but are not identical. Modern theories distinguish descriptive questions about what societies treat as private from normative questions about what ought to be protected. Some approaches value privacy intrinsically; others value it because it enables dignity, autonomy, intimacy, trust, self-expression, or social relationships. Access-based theories emphasize protection from unwanted observation or intrusion, while control-based theories emphasize authority over access, information, spaces, or decisions. A major alternative, contextual integrity, evaluates information flows according to social contexts and their norms. The entry surveys criticisms of privacy. Reductionists argue that privacy claims can be explained through other rights. Economic critics ask whether privacy rules promote efficient uses of information. Communitarian critics emphasize shared practices and duties, while feminist critics challenge the assumption that the domestic sphere is naturally private and show how privacy can both protect freedom and conceal domination. Contemporary debates concern datafication, workplace monitoring, health apps, group privacy, surveillance, democracy, cultural variation, racism, colonial power, and conflicts with security or health. The entry does not resolve these disputes, but shows why privacy remains central to personal, social, legal, and political life.
key_ideas: The meaning of privacy is historically variable and cannot be captured by one definition accepted by everyone.
Privacy has at least three important dimensions: decisional, informational, and local.
The public/private boundary is conventional rather than simply natural; it is shaped by social practices, law, culture, and power.
Technology changes privacy by enabling continuous observation, data collection, profiling, and influence, not merely by adding new gadgets.
Critics disagree about whether privacy is a distinct right, an economic concern, a community practice, or a protection for individual freedom.
Privacy has social and democratic value because it supports trust, relationships, participation, and the ability to deliberate without constant surveillance.
summaries.why_it_matters: Privacy is not only about hiding secrets. It affects how people form relationships, present themselves, make decisions, and participate as citizens. Data systems can classify and influence people even when no single fact is secret. At the same time, privacy rules can be distributed unequally or used to shield harm. Careful thinking about privacy therefore requires asking what is being protected, from whom, under which norms, and with what consequences for other people and social institutions.

important_terms.definition: A contested concept involving protection from unwanted access, control over information, private places, and authority over personal decisions.
A historical and political distinction between areas open to collective or governmental action and areas reserved for personal or domestic regulation.
Privacy concerning control over personal information, including who knows it, how it is communicated, and what uses are made of it.
Privacy concerning a person’s authority to make important choices and direct conduct without unjustified interference.
Privacy concerning physical or spatial withdrawal, especially the home and other places of seclusion.
The view that privacy claims can be explained in terms of other rights or interests, such as property, bodily security, or freedom from intrusion.
The view that privacy contains several related interests, such as information control, independence, self-expression, and relationships, without being reduced to only one of them.
A view that information is appropriate or inappropriate partly according to the social context, the people involved, the type of information, and the rules for transferring it.

questions_to_think_about: Does a person retain informational privacy when information is publicly visible but collected and analyzed at large scale?
Is control over personal data enough to explain privacy, or are access, dignity, relationships, and autonomy also needed?
When can protecting domestic privacy preserve injustice, and when can removing it create a different injustice?
Should security or public health automatically outweigh privacy, or must the values be balanced?
Can groups have privacy when profiling targets categories of people rather than identifiable individuals?

summaries.example: Jordan uses a video-sharing app. Jordan posts a funny dance for friends, but the app also records viewing habits, contacts, and location. Jordan might accept friends seeing one kind of information while objecting to an advertiser, school, or government receiving it. This shows why privacy is not simply “keeping everything secret.” It involves expectations about people, purposes, and kinds of information.
summaries.summary: Privacy is a complicated idea about having some control over access to people, places, choices, and information. The entry traces several histories: the distinction between household life and public political life, the rise of concern about personal information, and the development of legal protections. These histories show that the line between public and private is made by social rules and can change. Philosophers disagree about the value and structure of privacy. Some say privacy is really a collection of other protections, such as property or freedom from being watched. Others argue that the different cases are connected and that privacy itself matters because it supports dignity, independence, intimacy, trust, and self-expression. Three useful dimensions are decisional privacy, informational privacy, and local privacy. Modern technologies make the issue especially urgent. Phones, apps, cameras, and data systems can monitor people, create profiles, and send information into new settings. One approach asks whether each flow of information fits the expectations of its context. The entry also discusses criticism from communitarian and feminist perspectives. Communities may shape what privacy means, but community traditions can restrict individuals. Treating the home as private can protect family life, yet it can also prevent attention to abuse or inequality. Current debates therefore ask how privacy should be balanced with safety, health, security, free expression, and accountability, and how unequal power affects who receives privacy protection.
key_ideas: People have understood privacy differently in different historical periods and cultures.
Privacy may protect information, decisions, relationships, and places, so one definition may not cover every case.
Digital technology allows organizations to collect data, combine it into profiles, and use it to predict or influence behavior.
The private sphere is not automatically fair: privacy at home has sometimes hidden unequal treatment, especially of women.
Critics disagree about whether privacy is a separate right or a name for several other rights and interests.
Privacy can benefit communities and democracy, not only isolated individuals.
summaries.why_it_matters: Privacy helps people develop friendships, try out ideas, make personal decisions, and take part in public life without being constantly watched. It also affects fairness because companies and governments may have much more information and power than ordinary people. Studying privacy helps us notice that sharing is not always the same as giving permission for every later use.

important_terms.definition: Protection from unwanted attention or interference, including control over information, personal choices, relationships, and physical spaces.
The boundary between activities open to society or government and activities treated as personal, domestic, or self-directed.
The ability to decide what personal information is shared, with whom, and for what purpose.
Protection for personal choices and actions, including decisions about one’s life and body.
Protection for a physical place of withdrawal, especially a home or room.
The idea that privacy is not one simple thing but a set of connected interests.
The view that privacy concerns can be reduced to other rights, such as property rights or protection from bodily intrusion.
The idea that information should move according to the expectations and rules of its particular social setting.

questions_to_think_about: If you post something for friends, is it reasonable for an app to sell it to advertisers?
Why might a person want privacy even when they are doing nothing wrong?
Can a private home be both a safe place and a place where unfair treatment is hidden?
Should a government collect location data during a health emergency? What limits might be needed?
Why might privacy matter for democracy and free discussion?
